column4: A building founded on taqwa and God’s pleasure stands opposite one on a collapsing cliff that carries its builder into Hell; the ayah contains the section’s foundation, brink, fall, and fiery end in one scene.
The believers had stood on the lip of a pit of fire and God rescued them from it, directly staging the section’s person drawn safely away from the well-mouth.
The saved speaker tells his former companion, تَرْدِينِ, that he nearly caused his ruin; this is the same ر د ي fall as the source word تَرَدَّىٰ, now understood from above after a narrow escape.
The garden-dweller looks down and sees his companion in the middle of Hell; it supplies the high vantage and downward gaze that make the near-fall named in 37:56 visible.
The speaker credits his Lord’s grace for not being among those brought to punishment, completing 37:56’s claim that his foot was almost drawn into ruin but was spared.
Moses is warned not to let a denier who follows desire turn him from the Hour, فَتَرْدَىٰ; the same ر د ي root makes heedless appetite a route to destruction.
ٱلْمُتَرَدِّيَةُ is an animal killed by a fall; this concrete legal use of ر د ي preserves the bodily plunge inside the source ayah’s moral ruin.
One who worships on an edge reverses himself when tested and loses both worlds; unstable worship turns the brink into the face-first reversal imagined by the section.
The person has not attempted the steep ascent, making moral choice an upward exertion opposite the source section’s unchecked downward roll.
Freeing a neck is one answer to what the steep ascent is, so release accomplished through expenditure becomes an actual upward route.
Feeding on a day of hunger continues the definition of the ascent begun in 90:11, matching the section’s claim that wealth given away carries one upward.
The orphaned relative identifies one recipient of the feeding that constitutes the steep ascent, giving the section’s upward use of wealth a concrete human object.
The destitute person in the dust completes the ascent’s feeding scene; elevation is achieved by bending toward the person already brought low.
The command to glorify the name of the Lord ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ identifies God as the true bearer of the height toward which the source giver turns.

In the setting of spending, the command not to cast yourselves into destruction gives the section’s definition “exposing oneself to ruin” an ethical counterpart: give and do good rather than throw yourself over the edge.
The ayah contrasts one walking fallen upon his face with one walking upright on a straight path; it is the section’s heedless walker and two directions rendered as rival postures.
The associator is likened to one fallen from the sky, then snatched by birds or hurled far by wind; this is an exposed, irrecoverable plunge into destruction.
Someone asks to be spared a trial, yet the ayah says he has already fallen into it and Hell encompasses the disbelievers; the supposed escape is itself the hidden snare and fall.
The one whose scales are light has an abyss as his destination, making the ruined person’s end a downward place rather than merely an abstract loss.
The abyss named in 101:9 is identified as a raging fire, completing the section’s trajectory from fall to burning.
Abu Lahab’s wealth and earnings do not avail him, an exceptionally close restatement of money failing precisely before the fiery outcome in 111:3.
He will يَصْلَىٰ a flaming fire after his wealth fails in 111:2; the same ص ل ي verb and the same wealth-to-fire sequence meet the source image.
The condemned person says his wealth did not avail him, turning the source’s third-person verdict about useless property into the fallen person’s own recognition.
The command then says to make him enter and burn in Hell, so 69:28’s useless wealth culminates in the same fiery destination carried by source يَصْلَىٰهَا.
The slanderer gathers and repeatedly counts wealth; this identifies the possession clutched just before the casting described in 104:4.
He supposes his wealth has made him enduring, exposing the precise illusion refuted by the source claim that wealth cannot save at the fall.
He will be cast into the Crusher, converting confidence in accumulated wealth into a sudden downward and destructive movement.
The Crusher is God’s kindled fire, completing 104:4’s casting and joining the section’s fall to its burning snare.
From the Heights, men call to arrogant people and ask what their amassed company and pride availed them; height, downward recognition, and failed worldly resources converge here.
When the people on the Heights have their eyes turned toward the people of the Fire, they pray not to be placed with them; this supplies the fearful downward gaze behind 7:48.
The false gods and the strayers are tumbled headlong into Hell, a direct infernal version of the source’s rolling fall.
God attacks plotters’ building at its foundations so the roof falls on them from above; fabricated security becomes the mechanism of its owner’s collapse.
Qarun and his house are swallowed into the earth, and neither his party nor he can save him; his great property and support are powerless at a literal downward ruin.
Those who had desired Qarun’s station recognize after his swallowing that worldly provision is no proof of success; the witnessed fall corrects their valuation of wealth.
The rich man’s produce is destroyed and his trellises lie collapsed while he regrets what he spent on them; possessed wealth and its supporting structure fail together.
After the garden’s collapse, he has no party to help him apart from God and cannot help himself, echoing the source’s insistence that what is in the falling man’s hand cannot arrest ruin.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to God, whereas faith and righteous action do; it explicitly separates owned means from the genuine upward approach.
On the Day of Resurrection neither wealth nor children benefit, giving the source’s “wealth does not avail” its final-day scope.
The disbelievers’ wealth and children will not avail them against God, and they become fuel for the Fire; failed resources lead directly to burning.
Wealth and children do not avail the disbelievers against God, and they are companions of the Fire; it repeats the section’s useless possession and fiery destination.
Neither wealth nor children avail the opponents of God, and the ayah assigns them to the Fire; worldly protection proves unable to prevent the final descent.
The punishment is لَظَىٰ, a blazing fire, recalling the source surah’s fiery setting and opening a sequence in which hoarded wealth ends there.
The blaze strips away the scalp, making the bodily exposure to ruin in 70:15 concrete rather than metaphorical.
The blaze calls the one who turned his back and withdrew, a grim counter-call to the section’s summons upward toward the Most High.
The person summoned by the blaze amassed wealth and stored it away, directly joining hoarding to the fiery end described in 70:15.
Those who spend seeking God’s pleasure are like a garden on elevated ground; the act of giving and the physical height become one image of secure increase.
The ayah says worthy expenditure is made seeking only God’s Face, directly matching the source giver’s motive in facing the Most High.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, meeting the steep ascent’s concrete use of possessions.
They explain that they feed only for God’s Face and want neither reward nor thanks, closely paralleling giving without repayment while seeking the Lord’s Face.
Giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their due is attributed to those who desire God’s Face; expenditure is again directed upward by its object of desire.
Those who remain patient seeking their Lord’s Face and spend from His provision are promised the final abode, combining motive, giving, and destination.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth, freeing slaves, and culminates in calling such people the Godfearing; it joins the ascent of 90:13 with the source’s giving ٱلْأَتْقَى.
The Helpers prefer others despite their own need, and those protected from their soul’s greed succeed; being guarded from the inner snare is expressed through giving.
The command joins taqwa, obedience, and spending, then names protection from one’s own greed as success; it maps the source Godfearing giver’s safe direction.
Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, making orientation toward divine height a movement enacted by deeds.
The believer who comes with righteous deeds receives ٱلدَّرَجَـٰتُ ٱلْعُلَىٰ, “the highest degrees”; moral action ends in the height signified by the source root ع ل و.
Those for whom the best decree has preceded are kept far away from Hell, a direct semantic parallel to the Godfearing person being pulled aside from it.
Those kept far from Hell do not even hear its sound and remain amid what they desire, showing the completeness of the removal asserted in 21:101.
God saves those who were Godfearing and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling there, closely paralleling ٱلْأَتْقَى being removed from the Fire while its opposite remains.
God saves those with taqwa in their place of triumph, with evil neither touching nor grieving them; their precaution culminates in divine extraction from danger.
Whoever has punishment turned away from him that Day has received mercy, a direct nonlexical equivalent of being moved aside from the threatened fire.
The servants of the Merciful ask that Hell’s punishment be turned away from them, voicing the movement away from fire that source وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا promises.
The garden-dwellers rejoice because their Lord protected them from the punishment of Hell, supplying the safe outcome after removal from the brink.
Believers are commanded to guard themselves and their families from a Fire, converting the section’s rescue image into an imperative of prevention.
Criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire; face, involuntary movement, and fiery ruin fuse as they do in the section’s use of 22:11.
Those bringing evil are cast face-first into the Fire, a concise infernal enactment of downward direction and the unprotected face.
A person can only shield the face from the worst punishment, a posture showing that no possession or ordinary defense remains available at the fall.
The “people of the trench” introduces a literal excavated pit whose fire is named in 85:5, strongly echoing the section’s fiery chasm.
The trench is filled with fuel-fed fire, joining the section’s two objects—the pit and the blaze—in one scene.
The persecutors sit above the fiery trench, supplying an upper edge and a lower fire, though here the moral guilt belongs to those safely seated above.
They witness what they do to the believers below; this reverses the section’s moral alignment by placing guilty spectators at the height and faithful victims at the fire.
God commands the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham, showing that the apparent fiery snare has no power over the person whom God preserves.
Abraham’s people propose killing or burning him, but God saves him from the fire; deliberate casting is answered by divine removal.
God protects the believing man from the evils of Pharaoh’s plots, while the next ayah says punishment encloses Pharaoh’s people; rescue and entrapment divide the two directions.
Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening and then admitted to harsher punishment, completing 40:45’s reversal of plotter and protected believer.
God makes the disbelievers’ word the lowest while God’s word is the highest, ٱلْعُلْيَا; the section’s vertical axis becomes an explicit judgment between false and true claims.
The final home is for those who do not desire عُلُوًّا, self-exaltation on earth; it distinguishes ascent toward the Most High from making oneself high over others.
Satan is ordered to descend because arrogance has no place in the garden; attempted self-height directly produces abasement and downward removal.
Pharaoh declares himself the people’s ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ lord; the source section marks this as the counterfeit seizure of a height that belongs to God.
God seizes Pharaoh with the punishment of the latter and former after his claim in 79:24, showing false height converted into comprehensive downfall.
Humanity is returned to the lowest of the low, a downward outcome that gives explicit language to the section’s opposite pole.
Believers who act rightly are excepted from the reduction in 95:5 and receive an unfailing reward, defining the route that escapes the low destination.
Hypocrites occupy the lowest depth of the Fire, locating moral duplicity at the bottom of the section’s vertical axis.
Pharaoh عَلَا in the land and divided its people, so the root ع ل و denotes oppressive self-elevation rather than the true height sought in the source.
Pharaoh orders a tower built so he may ascend toward Moses’ God while asserting no other deity; fabricated physical ascent exposes the falsity of his claim to height.
Pharaoh asks Haman to build him a tower so he may reach the routes, beginning an attempted ascent toward the heavens that 40:37 exposes as delusion.
Pharaoh proposes looking upon Moses’ God from the tower, but his plot ends only in ruin; self-authorized ascent becomes another path to destruction.
God asks Iblis whether he has grown arrogant or counts himself among ٱلْعَالِينَ; the root of height is interrogated as a false status claimed against divine command.
Believers are told not to weaken or grieve because they are ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ if faithful; true height is made conditional on faith rather than possession or self-claim.
God tells the fearful Moses that he is ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ, turning height into divine reassurance before confrontation with deceptive power.
Believers are told not to lose heart while they are ٱلْأَعْلَوْنَ and God is with them; the source root marks a conferred moral position rather than self-exaltation.
God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees, explicitly making faithful response the cause of upward rank.
God raises Idris to مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا, a high station; this is a positive personal elevation from the same ع ل و family, though without the source’s brink scene.
God is Lord of the ascents, locating true upward ways with Him and preparing the actual ascent described in 70:4.
The angels and Spirit ascend to God, supplying a cosmic literalization of the upward direction owned by the Lord of ascents in 70:3.
تَعَالَوْا calls the People of the Book to a common word of worshipping God alone; the source dictionary’s “come upward” form becomes a summons from false lordship to the true Lord.
When told تَعَالَوْا to God’s revelation and the Messenger, hypocrites turn away; the upward call and the refusing downward orientation are staged together.
The call تَعَالَوْا to revelation and the Messenger is refused for inherited custom even when the fathers lacked knowledge and guidance, showing what keeps people from answering the upward summons.
When told تَعَالَوْا so the Messenger may seek forgiveness for them, the hypocrites turn their heads and withdraw arrogantly; refusal of the root’s upward call is itself a claim of false height.
The Prophet says تَعَالَوْا and calls hearers to listen to what their Lord has forbidden; the dictionary form identified in the section introduces a concrete summons into divine guidance.
The hypocrites are told تَعَالَوْا to fight in God’s way or defend, but profess inability and retreat; the upward-form call discloses their contrary direction.

تَعَالَوْا summons both sides and their families to the decisive mutual invocation after knowledge has come; it exemplifies the call-form derived from height, though its immediate scene is disputation.

The form تَعَالَيْنَ calls the Prophet’s wives to receive provision and a gracious release if they choose worldly life and adornment; it is a specific boundary case where the root-form “come” introduces separation, while 33:29 states the higher alternative.

Choosing God, His Messenger, and the final home instead of worldly adornment completes the fork opened by تَعَالَيْنَ in 33:28 and clarifies which choice corresponds to the section’s upward orientation.
A garden-dweller recalls that he had a close companion, identifying the person later seen below and accused in 37:56 of nearly causing his ruin.
The speaker asks his companions whether they will look, initiating the downward view into Hell completed in 37:55.
The question “what will make you know the steep ascent?” pauses over the upward obstacle before 90:13–16 define it through liberation and feeding.
Faith, mutual patience, and mercy continue the description of those who negotiate the ascent, preventing its material acts from being detached from a believing community.
Those who complete the qualities of the ascent are companions of the right, assigning the upward course a final side and company.
Those who reject the signs are companions of the left, the opposing company to the ascent’s people in 90:18.
A closed fire surrounds the rejecting company, completing the steep-ascent passage with the trapped fiery destination opposite liberation and feeding.

Joseph’s brother proposes placing him in the hidden depth of a well, directly activating the well-mouth object behind the source dictionary definition, though Joseph is thrown rather than heedlessly falling.
The brothers carry out their agreement to put Joseph in the well’s hidden depth; the image supplies the downward destination without making it his moral ruin.
A caravan lowers its bucket and draws Joseph out as found treasure; upward rescue from the literal well reverses the source image of an unrecoverable fall.
The believing companion warns that the rich man’s garden may become a bare slippery ground, foreshadowing the collapse of owned security in 18:42.
He also warns that its water may sink so deep that the owner cannot retrieve it; apparent command of property ends at an inaccessible depth.

The summary of destroyed peoples includes one whom God caused the earth to swallow and insists none could escape the consequence of wrongdoing; Qarun’s fall becomes one form in a larger pattern of self-caused ruin.
A barrier separates the two destinations and men stand on the Heights recognizing each group, establishing the elevated threshold from which 7:47–48 look toward the Fire.
The people once denied mercy by the arrogant are told to enter the Garden without fear or grief, reversing the judgment voiced by those whose gathering avails nothing in 7:48.
Light scales identify whose destination becomes the abyss in 101:9; the ayah gives the moral measure preceding the downward end.
The question about the abyss holds the reader at its edge before 101:11 discloses that it is fire.
The question about the Crusher interrupts the casting scene so that 104:6 can identify the destination as God’s fire.
The fire rises over the hearts, showing that the punishment into which the wealth-counter is cast reaches the inward seat of his false confidence.
The fire is closed over them, giving the source’s snare an infernal analogue from which the caught person cannot step aside.
Extended columns complete the enclosure of 104:8, reinforcing the impossibility of escape after the casting.
The condemned person says his authority has perished after admitting that wealth failed in 69:28; every secondary means of arresting the fall has vanished.
The order to seize and shackle him removes freedom of movement immediately before the command to burn him in 69:31.
Abraham’s opponents command that he be burned to support their gods; the intended fiery trap is the one God overturns in 21:69.
The plotters intend harm, but God makes them the greatest losers; the agents who prepare another’s destruction inherit the downward outcome.
